title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Tool‑Augmented Agent vs LLM‑Only Generation for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration
abstract: We ran a fully preregistered paired experiment (study_id: cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) to test whether augmenting an LLM with a deterministic NetOps verifier and a lightweight topology simulator (tool‑augmented guarded pipeline) improves deterministic‑validator pass rates versus an LLM‑only baseline on synthetic intent→configuration tasks. Planned n=300 paired tasks (150 simple, 150 complex); 299 complete pairs were analyzable. Under the executed design (shared_initial_candidate generation semantics, see Methods), both conditions produced identical generated artifacts for the confirmatory set and identical deterministic‑validator pass counts (baseline 299/299, guarded 299/299). Paired difference = 0.00 (McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], 10k resamples). A preregistered sensitivity analysis treating technical failures as verifier‑failures (per the preregistration) yields the same paired difference. The run is internally reproducible and fully archived; because we used a shared initial candidate across conditions by design, the experiment assesses downstream verifier/tool effects on a shared LLM output rather than whether independent tool‑augmented generation changes model outputs. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, validator traces, analysis artifacts, and SHA‑256 hashes; we discuss the methodological implications, failure modes, and recommended follow‑ups (independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model replication, richer simulators).

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are proposed for intent‑driven NetOps tasks (intent→device configuration), but fluent outputs can be operationally unsafe unless grounded by validators or toolchains. Prior work explores intent translation, generate–validate–repair flows, and tool‑augmented agents for safer NetOps [see Related Work]. We preregistered and executed a paired study to answer: does augmenting an LLM with a deterministic NetOps verifier and topology‑aware simulator (guarded pipeline) increase deterministic‑validator pass rates versus an LLM‑only pipeline on matched synthetic intent tasks? We report a fully artifact‑anchored execution (study_id cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1), the exact preregistered estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), and the observed outcomes with deterministic provenance.
sections.related_work: Work on LLMs for network configuration and intent translation includes fine‑tuning and in‑context approaches [Nguyen Tu et al., 2024; PreConfig arXiv:2403.09369]; recent proposals study tool‑augmentation, verifier taxes, and runtime mechanisms that improve agent reliability [WeClaw 2026; Verifier Tax 2026]. Generate–validate–repair architectures and deterministic validators have been advocated to reduce outage‑inducing misconfigurations. Our study differs by preregistering a paired confirmatory design with full archival provenance and by executing a deterministic validator pipeline on synthetic intent tasks to produce reproducible, hash‑anchored outcomes.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen design. The complete preregistration (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1; preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0) fixed: primary estimand, sampling plan (300 paired tasks, 150 simple/150 complex), metrics, validator, seeds, retry policy, and a crucial generation semantics decision: shared_initial_candidate (a single LLM generation reused across both conditions). Execution contract. Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model provider: openai_responses; declared_model_version: gpt-5-mini (see execution/model_configuration.json, SHA‑256 recorded in manifest). Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). Tasks and simulator. Tasks were drawn from a public synthetic topology/template pool; each task encodes initial and expected final states, allowed fields, and workflow constraints (examples: shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break). Data and provenance. All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and SHA‑256 hashes were recorded (see execution manifest and artifact hash manifest). Analysis plan. Primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar and bootstrap paired CI, 10k resamples, seed=1729). Sensitivity analysis treating technical failures as verifier‑fail was preregistered and executed. Deterministic accounting. The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation confirm completed_episode_count=598, failed_episode_count=2, complete_pair_count=299; all counts and hashes are archived and are authoritative.
sections.results: Execution outcomes. Planned episodes: 600 (300 pairs). Completed: 598 episodes; failed: 2 episodes; complete analyzable pairs: 299. Primary confirmatory outcome: deterministic validator pass counts — baseline 299/299, guarded 299/299. Contingency table (complete pairs): n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference (guarded−baseline)=0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.0. Bootstrap (10,000 resamples; seed=1729) 95% percentile CI for paired difference = [0.00, 0.00]. Sensitivity treating preregistered failed runs as verifier‑failures: one pair had both episodes fail; assigning those as failures produces n11=299, n00=1 and leaves discordant counts zero—paired difference remains 0.00 and the test remains non‑informative for improvement. Missingness and exclusions. No confirmatory exclusions for contamination were flagged. Representative artifacts. Representative shared initial candidates and scoring JSONs are archived: e.g., execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256: 8f38c8...), execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256: cefa63...), and the validator traces shown in the analysis bundle illustrate the validation workflow.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and limits of inference. The observed null difference (0.00) is a valid, artifact‑grounded outcome of the preregistered, executed protocol. However, by design we reused a single shared_initial_candidate across both conditions; the run therefore evaluated downstream verifier/tool processing of an identical LLM output rather than whether tool‑augmentation leads to different (and safer) LLM generations. Consequently the null result should not be interpreted as evidence that tool‑augmented agents cannot improve generation‑level outcomes; it only shows that, for the shared LLM candidate set used in this run, downstream verification/tooling did not change verifier pass/fail results. Methodological lesson: shared‑candidate semantics reduce generation variance and increase internal control, but they can mask generation‑level improvements—future confirmatory designs that aim to test agentic generation should preregister independent per‑condition generation and account for increased sample size and model‑call budgets. Operational implications. Deterministic validators and light simulators are useful for traceability and failure diagnosis; they provide concrete validator traces (command parsing, final_state snapshots, difficulty annotations) that aid debugging and reproducibility. Reproducibility. All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, execution manifest, and SHA‑256 hashes are archived and form the authoritative record for all numeric results reported here. Threats to validity. Construct validity: synthetic tasks and a lightweight simulator approximate but do not fully reproduce production complexity or vendor CLI richness. External validity: single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies limit generalization. Internal validity: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate design constrains inference as described above. Conclusion validity: achieved confirmatory sample and preregistered power assumptions were respected; however, because both conditions observed identical generated artifacts, the primary test is insensitive to generation‑level effects.
sections.conclusion: We present a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment comparing a verifier‑anchored guarded pipeline against an LLM‑only baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Observed verifier‑pass rates were identical in the executed design (299/299 each; paired difference 0.00, p=1.0). The result is definitive for the executed protocol but does not adjudicate whether independent tool‑augmented generation would improve outcomes. We release the preregistration, raw responses, scoring and validator traces, and a full SHA‑256 artifact manifest to support reproducibility. Future confirmatory work should (a) preregister independent per‑condition generation semantics, (b) replicate across multiple LLMs and task banks, and (c) employ richer simulation of runtime interactions and vendor CLIs to increase external validity.

disclosure_statement: This paper and all reported results were produced by an autonomous, post‑lock execution run governed by the frozen master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Preregistration: study_id cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0) was frozen before execution. LLM(s) used: declared_model_version gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; provider recorded as openai_responses). Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Execution contract and key design choices: paired within‑task design with planned 300 paired tasks; maximum_model_calls 600; and the preregistered generation semantics used in this run were shared_initial_candidate (a single LLM generation reused across baseline and guarded conditions). The shared_initial_candidate decision is recorded in the preregistration and execution manifest and is central to interpreting the results: the experiment tests downstream verifier/tool processing of identical LLM outputs rather than testing whether the guarded agent would produce different initial generations when permitted. Tools permitted: deterministic validator, lightweight topology simulator, and up to one repair call per task per the preregistered retry policy. All raw model outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, execution logs, and SHA‑256 artifact hashes are archived in the execution bundle (see execution_manifest paths within the supplied artifacts). Two technical failures occurred (failed_episode_count=2); these failures, the missingness summary, and a preregistered sensitivity analysis that treats failures as verifier‑fails are reported and archived. No manual human editing of the manuscript technical content occurred after the autonomy lock; all manuscript numbers and claims are grounded in the archived execution and analysis artifacts listed in the bundle.
limitations: Preregistered execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (single LLM generation reused across baseline and guarded). That design makes this run an assessment of downstream verifier/tool effects given identical generated artifacts, and it precludes inference about whether independent tool‑augmented generation would have produced safer outputs.
Tasks were synthetic and evaluated in a lightweight simulator; external validity to heterogeneous vendor CLIs, complex runtime state, and production NetOps telemetry is limited.
Only a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) was exercised; results do not generalize across model families or sizes.
The deterministic validator approximates operational checks but cannot capture all real runtime side effects or hardware/software heterogeneity.

Because both conditions observed identical generated artifacts in the confirmatory set, the primary statistical test is insensitive to generation‑level effects and cannot settle broader claims about agentic generation benefits.
